extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional law, and comparative politics
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the advantages, dangers, and institutional safeguards relating to an elective chief executive (the President) and the necessity, organization, and independence of a federal judiciary in a republic. Discusses electoral mode, election crises, re-eligibility, and federal court structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of the elective system increase with executive prerogative
rubrics_metrics.description: The dangers of the system of election applied to the head of the executive government of a great people ... may be more or less formidable in proportion to the place which the executive power occupies, and to the importance it possesses in the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the executive possesses greater privileges and influence, the temptation to ambition and the capacity for factional seizure of power rise. Thus making a powerful executive elective is especially hazardous; safe application of an elective system requires circumscribing executive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favorable circumstances for an elective executive
rubrics_metrics.description: Before we can discuss the absolute advantages of the elective system we must make preliminary inquiries as to whether the geographical position, the laws, the habits, the manners, and the opinions of the people amongst whom it is to be introduced will admit of the establishment of a weak and dependent executive government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elective executive is feasible where physical/security environment and social/political habits permit a weak, subordinate executive — e.g., absence of hostile neighbors, a people practiced in freedom, and institutions that do not demand constant strong executive intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: If making hereditary royalty elective, restrict prerogatives progressively
rubrics_metrics.description: To reduce hereditary royalty to the condition of an elective authority, the only means that I am acquainted with are to circumscribe its sphere of action beforehand, gradually to diminish its prerogatives, and to accustom the people to live without its protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitioning from strong hereditary monarchy to an elective head requires deliberately limiting the executive's scope, removing prerogatives over time, and socializing the populace to less reliance on executive protection to avoid instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective systems introduce instability, mitigated by limited executive power
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the principal vices of the elective system is that it always introduces a certain degree of instability into the internal and external policy of the State. But this disadvantage is less sensibly felt if the share of power vested in the elected magistrate is small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the preponderant power rests with other bodies (e.g., a deliberative assembly), frequent change in the executive causes less systemic variation; for stability ensure that elected executive's practical authority is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections create a national crisis proportional to internal/external dangers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the prerogatives of the executive power may be, the period which immediately precedes an election and the moment of its duration must always be considered as a national crisis, which is perilous in proportion to the internal embarrassments and the external dangers of the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nearer a nation is to internal instability or external threat, the more dangerous the election interregnum becomes. Designers should minimize the risks of suspended governance at election times (via quick procedures, limited prerogatives, or continuity measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral college: delegate to a special electoral body to reduce delay and corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The means by which it was proposed to obviate this second obstacle was to delegate the electoral powers of the nation to a body of representatives... It was therefore established that every State should name a certain number of electors, who in their turn should elect the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a smaller, special body of electors (rather than the legislature or a mass popular assembly) increases the likelihood of a decisive majority, reduces exposure of legislators to electioneering corruption, and expedites selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electors should vote on the same day and transmit sealed individual votes
rubrics_metrics.description: It was determined that the electors should all vote upon the same day, without being convoked to the same place... they transmit to the central government the list of their individual votes, and not the mere result of the vote of the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simultaneous voting and transmission of individual sealed ballots prevent prolonged agitation and local cabals; avoid aggregating only state-majority results at the center to preserve record of individual elector choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallback: House elects President among top three if no majority
rubrics_metrics.description: If none of the candidates has a majority, the House of Representatives then proceeds immediately to elect a President, but with the condition that it must fix upon one of the three candidates who have the highest numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a clear, fast constitutional mechanism for unresolved electoral majorities that limits the range of candidates and returns the decision to a representative body to avoid indefinite suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller number of electors increases chance of majority and prudent choice
rubrics_metrics.description: This mode of election rendered a majority more probable; for the fewer the electors are, the greater is the chance of their coming to a final decision. It also offered an additional probability of a judicious choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional designers should balance representativeness and decisiveness: reducing elector numbers can produce timely, considered outcomes, though it requires checks to preserve legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election periods slow government action and produce a break in administration
rubrics_metrics.description: In elective States, on the contrary, the wheels of government cease to act, as it were, of their own accord at the approach of an election... The head of the executive government is wholly occupied by the coming struggle; his future plans are doubtful; he can undertake nothing new...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and mitigate administrative paralysis around elections (e.g., limit timing, delegate continuity authorities) because executive preoccupation with re-election or succession can stagnate governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-eligibility of the executive encourages corruption and pandering
rubrics_metrics.description: When the head of the State can be re-elected these evils rise to a great height... the representative of the executive descends into the combat, he borrows the strength of the government for his own purposes... the cares of government dwindle into second-rate importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting immediate re-election concentrates state resources in electoral contests and incentivizes incumbents to subordinate public duty to electoral advantage; consider ineligibility or term limits to preserve executive independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's weakness: subordinating authority to majority's fleeting desires
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural evil of democracy is that it subordinates all authority to the slightest desires of the majority — The re-election of the President encourages this evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional mechanisms should restrain transient majorities from capturing long-term public authority; structures like independent chambers, vetoes, or non-re-eligibility can check majority caprice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government requires a national judiciary to enforce laws
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal government stands in greater need of the support of judicial institutions than any other, because it is naturally weak and exposed to formidable opposition... The Union, therefore, required a national judiciary to enforce the obedience of the citizens to the laws, and to repel the attacks which might be directed against them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A federation should create federal courts with jurisdiction to apply national laws uniformly; relying solely on state tribunals risks partiality and uneven enforcement of federal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: State courts are inadequate for enforcing federal law due to partiality and multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: To entrust the execution of the laws of the Union to tribunals instituted by these political bodies would be to allow foreign judges to preside over the nation... the number... of the tribunals of the States rendered them unfit for the service of the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform interpretation and enforcement require separate federal tribunals because state courts are 'foreign' (originating in distinct political bodies) and their multiplicity could produce conflicting fundamental-law interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and jurisdictional design of federal courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The American legislators therefore agreed to create a federal judiciary power to apply the laws of the Union... The entire judicial power of the Union was centred in one tribunal, which was denominated the Supreme Court... inferior courts were appended to it, which were empowered to decide causes of small importance without appeal, and with appeal causes of more magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a hierarchical federal court system: a supreme national court for final say on important matters, with inferior district/circuit courts handling lesser matters and appeals to the supreme court to manage caseload and uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence via appointment process, tenure, and immutable salary
rubrics_metrics.description: The members of the Supreme Court are named neither by the people nor the legislature, but by the President of the United States, acting with the advice of the Senate. In order to render them independent of the other authorities, their office was made inalienable; and it was determined that their salary, when once fixed, should not be altered by the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure impartiality, appoint federal judges by executive nomination with legislative advice/consent, grant life or inalienable tenure, and protect compensation from political manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court's competence over facts and law (contrast with some civil-law courts)
rubrics_metrics.description: It will be observed that no analogy exists between the Supreme Court of the United States and the French Cour de Cassation, since the latter only hears appeals on questions of law. The Supreme Court decides upon the evidence of the fact as well as upon the law of the case...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether the supreme tribunal will re-decide facts as well as law; a supreme court that reexamines facts performs a different function from a cassation-style court and affects case-processing and finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of jury in federal courts similar to states
rubrics_metrics.description: The jury was introduced into the Federal Courts in the same manner, and in the same cases, as into the courts of the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If adopting jury trial at the federal level, align its scope with existing state practice to preserve procedural familiarity and legitimacy, unless deliberate harmonization changes are intended.
